facts.fact_text: On 17 May 2012 Mr Romanov took part in the 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg.
The 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg on 17 May 2012 had been authorised by the local authorities.
The 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg on 17 May 2012 marked the International Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia.
On 11 January 2013 Mr Lebedev and Mr Nasonov notified the authorities in Voronezh of their intent to hold a demonstration involving about fifty participants on 20 January 2013.
The planned demonstration on 20 January 2013 in Voronezh was against the enactment of the law banning 'propaganda of non-traditional sexual relations'.
The authorities in Voronezh authorised the demonstration planned for 20 January 2013.

On 29 June 2013 Mr Starov, Ms Pitenova, Mr Fedorov and Mr Prokopenko took part in a demonstration involving about eighty participants in St Petersburg aimed at drawing attention to violations of the rights of LGBTI people in Russia.
The local authorities had been notified in advance of the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg.
On 12 October 2013 Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina intended to take part in a demonstration in St Petersburg to mark Coming Out Day.
The police did not intervene when counter-demonstrators started insulting the participants in the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012.
About forty police officers were present at the site of the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh on 20 January 2013 but did not intervene.
All the participants in the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh on 20 January 2013 had to stop the demonstration and leave.
The police present at the scene of the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg did not intervene when counter-demonstrators attacked the participants.

The police did not intervene when counter-demonstrators pushed Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina and prevented them from proceeding to the venue of the demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.

At 1.55 p.m. on 12 October 2013, five minutes before the demonstration started, the police began apprehending the participants, including Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina, on the grounds that they had used foul language.
Mr Fedorov and Ms Levina complained that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully, before the start of the authorised demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.

The case concerns the respondent State's alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation into incidents of homophobic acts of violence against the applicants.

Between July 2013 and December 2015 the police repeatedly refused to open a criminal investigation into battery committed for hate motives under Article 116 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation in relation to the attacks of 29 June 2013, citing a 'hostile attitude of people of heterosexual orientation towards members of the LGBTI community'.

Following the last decision by the police on 23 December 2015 not to initiate a criminal investigation into the attacks of 29 June 2013, the police did not carry out the measures ordered by the prosecutor.
On 16 July 2014 the investigator suspended the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin on the grounds that the attackers could not be identified.
The investigators suspended and resumed the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin multiple times, most recently on 7 October 2017, without achieving any tangible results.
No criminal investigation was ever instituted in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on 14 October 2017.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should ensure effective, prompt and impartial investigations into alleged cases of crimes and other incidents where the sexual orientation or gender identity of the victim is reasonably suspected to have constituted a motive for the perpetrator.

The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance noted in its report CRI(2019)2 that the United Nations expressed concern about the fact that Article 63 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation on aggravating circumstances does not appear to have ever been applied to cases involving violence against LGBTI persons, in spite of a high number of such incidents.

In its concluding observations on the seventh periodic report of the Russian Federation of 28 April 2015 (CCPR/C/RUS/7), the United Nations Human Rights Committee expressed concern that Article 63 § 1 (e) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, recognising as aggravated circumstances the commission of an offence for reasons of 'hatred or enmity' or 'hate or hostility towards a given social group', does not appear to have ever been applied to cases involving violence against LGBTI individuals.

In its concluding observations CCPR/C/RUS/7, the United Nations Human Rights Committee stated that the Russian Federation should take all the steps necessary to ensure the investigation, prosecution and punishment of any act of violence motivated by the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity and apply the provisions of Article 63 § 1 (e) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation to such acts.
